# Jain-Krishna autocatalytic set model

`jain-krishna` · *Jain & Krishna, 1998-2002*

## Introduction

The Jain-Krishna model is a small mathematical model of how a network of
chemicals that help one another can arise from a random soup, grow, and later
collapse. Sanjay Jain and Sandeep Krishna, then at the Indian Institute of
Science in Bangalore, introduced it in 1998 and developed it in a series of
papers up to 2011. Their starting question, in the words of their 1998 paper,
was the "origin of such networks and their movement towards greater
complexity". The picture they had in mind is a pond on the early Earth, holding
a fixed number of kinds of molecules. The molecules speed up (catalyse) each
other's production. Now and then a storm, flood or tide washes out the rarest
kind and brings in a new one with different catalytic habits.

The model keeps only the bare bones of that picture. Each kind of molecule is a
node of a graph, and an arrow from A to B means "A catalyses the production of
B". Nothing else about the molecules is represented: not their structure, not
the raw materials they are made from. Populations follow from the graph, and
the least populated kind is repeatedly swapped for a new node with random
arrows. For a long time this goes nowhere. Then, by chance, a closed loop of
arrows appears (A makes B and B makes A), a so-called **autocatalytic set**, a
group of species that among them catalyse the production of every member. That
loop takes over the population, the rest of the graph reorganises around it,
and within a short time every species is part of one large cooperative
network. Later, a single replacement can bring the whole structure down.

It is a **simulation model**, and a deliberately idealised one: all catalytic
strengths are equal, the number of species is fixed, and no species may make
copies of itself. Its point is that cooperation and structure appear without
anyone selecting for them. Selection only removes the rarest species; the
structure comes from the chance appearance of an autocatalytic set. Jain and
Krishna also show that this happens on a short, predictable time scale, while
the structure it builds would be astronomically unlikely to arise at random.

Banzhaf and Yamamoto introduce it in their origin-of-life chapter, as a
simplification of Kauffman's autocatalytic sets (book §6.3.1), and discuss it
in detail in the chapter on constructive dynamical systems (§15.2.2–15.2.3).
There it serves as their main example of how novelty can enter a system whose
number of variables never changes. Its neighbours in the catalog are the
other autocatalytic-set models. [Kauffman autocatalytic
sets](kauffman-autocatalytic-sets.md) and [RAF sets](raf.md) ask whether a
random reaction network *contains* an autocatalytic set, without dynamics.
[Bagley and Farmer](bagley-farmer.md) run such a network with real mass-action
kinetics in a flow reactor. [Random catalytic
networks](random-catalytic-networks.md) give a fixed random catalytic network
its population dynamics. What `jain-krishna` adds is a second, slower dynamics
in which the network itself evolves under selection.

| at a glance | |
|---|---|
| **family** | evolutionary-dynamics |
| **kind** | generator |
| **type** | generator — an algorithm computes the network from the chemistry's arguments |
| **constructive** | yes — the species set grows at run time |

## How it works

### Two things change, at two speeds

The model has two kinds of variables. The **fast** ones are the relative
populations `x_i` of the species: fractions between 0 and 1 that always sum to
1. The **slow** ones are the arrows of the graph, written as a matrix `C` of
zeros and ones: `c_ij = 1` means species `j` catalyses the production of
species `i`. The simulation alternates between them: the populations are given
time to settle, then the graph changes a little, then the populations settle
again.

**Fast step: populations settle.** With the graph fixed, each species grows in
proportion to the populations of its catalysts, and everything is diluted at a
common rate that keeps the total at 1:

```
x_i' = Σ_j c_ij x_j  −  x_i Σ_k Σ_j c_kj x_j        (book eq. 15.7)
```

The first term is production; the second is the dilution flow. Jain and Krishna
(1998) justify the equation as a well-stirred reactor in which the raw
materials are plentiful and the uncatalysed reaction is negligible, so that
the rate at which `i` is made is simply proportional to how much of its
catalysts there is. In reaction form, each arrow is one catalytic reaction,
`X_j → X_j + X_i`, with rate constant 1.

Because the equation is linear apart from the normalisation, its end state can
be computed instead of simulated. It is the eigenvector of `C` that belongs to
the largest eigenvalue, the **Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue** `λ1` (for a
matrix of non-negative numbers, like `C`, this eigenvalue is real and at least
0, and its eigenvector has no negative entries). The value of `λ1` says what
kind of graph it is:

- `λ1 = 0`: the graph has no closed loop, only chains and trees. Populations
  then pile up at the ends of the longest chains.
- `λ1 ≥ 1`: the graph contains an autocatalytic set. The species with non-zero
  population in the end state form an autocatalytic set, the **dominant ACS**,
  and every other species dies out. The simplest ACS is a 2-cycle, and
  `λ1 = 1` for a simple cycle; more interlocking loops raise `λ1`.

A species' population in this end state is its "fitness".

**Slow step: the rarest species is replaced.** One of the species with the
smallest end-state population is picked at random and removed with all its
arrows. A new species takes its place, and each of its arrows, in and out, is
drawn afresh with the same probability `p` as in the initial random graph. No
species may catalyse itself. Then the fast step runs again.

### A worked example

The default run (its output is under *Using it in Chemart* below) returns the
initial random graph: 22 arrows
among 100 species, so most species are isolated and there is no loop. Asking
for 768 replacements (`graph_updates=768`) gives the first graph of this run
that contains a loop. These are the reactions of its dominant ACS:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("jain-krishna", seed=1, graph_updates=768)
acs = net.extras["analysis"]["attractor_support"]
for r in net.reactions:
    if set(r.reactants) & set(acs):
        print(r.to_text())
print({s: round(net.initial_state[s], 3) for s in acs})
```

```
X86 -> X86 + X18  [mass-action k=1.0]
X86 -> X86 + X47  [mass-action k=1.0]
X93 -> X93 + X86  [mass-action k=1.0]
X47 -> X47 + X93  [mass-action k=1.0]
{'X18': 0.25, 'X47': 0.25, 'X86': 0.25, 'X93': 0.25}
```

Read the arrows: `X47` makes `X93`, `X93` makes `X86`, and `X86` makes `X47`
again. That is a 3-cycle, a loop of three species that sustains itself.
`X86` also makes `X18`, which does not feed back into the loop: it is a
"parasite" living off the cycle, what Jain and Krishna call the *periphery*,
as opposed to the loop itself, the *core*. The eigenvalue is `λ1 = 1`, and the
four species share the whole population equally; the other 96 species have
population 0.

To check that this is really where the populations go, integrate eq. 15.7 for
this network from equal populations (this uses SciPy; Chemart itself ships no
simulator):

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

ids = [s.id for s in net.species]
idx = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(ids)}
links = [(idx[next(iter(r.reactants))], idx[(set(r.products) - set(r.reactants)).pop()])
         for r in net.reactions]                  # (catalyst j, product i)

def f(t, x):
    growth = np.zeros_like(x)
    for j, i in links:
        growth[i] += x[j]                         # X_j -> X_j + X_i at rate 1
    return growth - x * growth.sum()              # eq. 15.7: dilution keeps sum x = 1

x = solve_ivp(f, (0, 2000), np.full(len(ids), 1 / len(ids)), rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12).y[:, -1]
top = np.argsort(x)[::-1][:6]
print({ids[k]: round(float(x[k]), 4) for k in top})
```

```
{'X86': 0.25, 'X47': 0.25, 'X18': 0.25, 'X93': 0.25, 'X54': 0.0, 'X35': 0.0}
```

Now the consequence for the slow step. Every species outside the loop has
population 0, so the next replacement is always one of them: the loop is
protected. Each new species has a chance of receiving an arrow from the loop
or its periphery. If it does, it joins the dominant ACS; if not, it has
population 0 and will soon be replaced again. So the ACS can only grow, until
it covers the whole graph. After that the species being replaced must come
from inside the ACS, and if it happens to hold the structure together, many
species can die out in a single step. That is the whole mechanism behind the
three phases described under *Results*.

### Symbols used below

In the formal specification, `m` is the number of species (nodes) and `p` the
probability of each arrow, both initially and on every replacement. Note that
the 1998 paper writes `s` for the number of species and uses `m` for the mean
number of arrows per node, `p(s − 1)`; the book and Chemart use `m` for the
number of species. "Fast attractor" means the end state of the fast step.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). m nodes of a directed graph; only the CATALYTIC action is represented, not the underlying reactions

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: 1). c_ij = 1 means X_j catalyses the production of X_i: X_j -&gt; X_j + X_i ; x_i' = sum_j c_ij x_j - x_i sum_kj c_kj x_j

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time).

*How the population is bounded:* normalisation sum_i x_i = 1

Two timescales. Fast: integrate to the fixed point. Slow: remove a species with the smallest concentration, replace it with a fresh node whose in/out edges are redrawn with probability p, reset, repeat.

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("jain-krishna", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
jain-krishna: 100 species, 22 reactions, status=complete
provides: catalysts, flow, initial-state, rate-constants, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: analysis
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
X59 -> X59 + X5  [mass-action k=1.0]
X30 -> X30 + X14  [mass-action k=1.0]
X38 -> X38 + X14  [mass-action k=1.0]
X31 -> X31 + X26  [mass-action k=1.0]
X46 -> X46 + X33  [mass-action k=1.0]
X2 -> X2 + X45  [mass-action k=1.0]
X52 -> X52 + X45  [mass-action k=1.0]
X52 -> X52 + X49  [mass-action k=1.0]
… and 14 more
```

The default call above returns the **initial random graph**, before any
replacement (`graph_updates = 0`). With `m = 100` and `p = 0.0025` it is the
setting of the book's run (Figure 15.6, taken from Jain and Krishna 2003) and
of the middle run in the 1998 paper. Each arrow is one reaction
`X_j -> X_j + X_i` with `k = 1`, and the network carries a constant-total
outflow, which is the dilution term of eq. 15.7. The species are named `X1` to
`X100`; the names carry no meaning. `net.initial_state` holds the fast
attractor of the returned graph, and `net.extras["analysis"]` records:

- `perron_frobenius_eigenvalue`: `λ1` of the returned graph, 0 if it has no
  ACS;
- `attractor_support`: the species with non-zero population in the attractor
  (the dominant ACS when `λ1 ≥ 1`; see the caveat under *Results* for
  `λ1 = 0`);
- `graph_updates`: how many replacements were applied.

To get an evolved network, ask for replacements. Each one costs an eigenvalue
computation, under a millisecond at `m = 100`, so a few thousand take seconds:

```python
for n in (767, 768, 2000):
    net = chemart.generate_network("jain-krishna", seed=1, graph_updates=n)
    a = net.extras["analysis"]
    print(n, len(net.reactions), a["perron_frobenius_eigenvalue"], len(a["attractor_support"]))
```

```
767 51 0.0 100
768 54 0.9999999999999998 4
2000 114 0.9999999999999998 100
```

After 767 replacements there is still no loop; after 768 there is the 3-cycle
of the worked example; after 2000 the ACS has absorbed all 100 species and the
graph has 114 arrows, five times the initial 22.

The generator returns only the final graph. To watch the history, run the same
loop yourself. The script below reuses Chemart's `attractor` function and makes
the random draws in the same order as the generator, so it follows exactly the
run that `generate_network("jain-krishna", seed=1, graph_updates=n)` returns at
each `n`. It takes about five seconds:

```python
import numpy as np
from chemart.chemistries.jain_krishna import attractor

m, p = 100, 0.0025
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)              # the same stream as generate_network(seed=1)
C = (rng.random((m, m)) < p).astype(int)    # C[i, j] = 1: X_j catalyses X_i
np.fill_diagonal(C, 0)
for n in range(8001):
    lam, x = attractor(C)                   # fast timescale: the fixed point of eq. 15.7
    s1 = int((x > 1e-9).sum()) if lam > 1e-9 else 0
    if n % 500 == 0:
        print(f"n={n:5d}  lambda1={lam:.3f}  s1={s1:3d}  links={C.sum():3d}")
    r = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(x <= x.min() + 1e-12))   # slow timescale: a least-populated node
    C[r, :] = rng.random(m) < p                            # ... gets fresh random links
    C[:, r] = rng.random(m) < p
    C[r, r] = 0
```

```
n=    0  lambda1=0.000  s1=  0  links= 22
n=  500  lambda1=0.000  s1=  0  links= 58
n= 1000  lambda1=1.000  s1= 11  links= 30
n= 1500  lambda1=1.000  s1= 21  links= 44
n= 2000  lambda1=1.000  s1=100  links=114
n= 2500  lambda1=1.000  s1=  4  links= 30
n= 3000  lambda1=1.000  s1=  6  links= 31
n= 3500  lambda1=1.000  s1= 27  links= 48
n= 4000  lambda1=1.000  s1= 70  links= 95
n= 4500  lambda1=1.194  s1= 99  links=114
n= 5000  lambda1=1.000  s1=  5  links= 29
n= 5500  lambda1=1.000  s1= 18  links= 49
n= 6000  lambda1=1.000  s1=  4  links= 23
n= 6500  lambda1=1.000  s1= 15  links= 40
n= 7000  lambda1=1.000  s1= 75  links= 93
n= 7500  lambda1=1.000  s1= 16  links= 40
n= 8000  lambda1=1.000  s1= 16  links= 36
```

Here `s1` is the size of the dominant ACS. The ACS appears (between `n = 500`
and `1000`; in fact at 768), grows to span the graph by `n = 2000`, then
crashes and regrows several times. The value of 58 arrows at `n = 500`, well
above the initial 22, is not what the paper's random phase looks like; see
the caveat under *Results*.

Other settings, from the parameter table below:

- **`p`** sets the pace. The expected wait for the first ACS is about
  `1/(p² m)` replacements and the growth takes about `(1/p) ln m` more, so
  halving `p` quadruples the wait. The 1998 paper studied mean degrees
  `p(m − 1)` from 0.05 to 2.0; at mean degree 1 or more the initial graph
  usually contains a loop already and there is no random phase.
- **`m`** up to 300. Larger graphs are slower per replacement (an
  eigen-decomposition of an `m × m` matrix) and need more replacements.
- **`self_loops=True`** allows `c_ii = 1`, a species that catalyses its own
  production. The model forbids this on purpose, to show that collective
  self-replication arises without individual self-replicators; the switch is
  there to see what changes without that restriction.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `m` | `int` | `100` | structural | number of nodes (the state-space dimension stays constant) <br>`2` … `300` |
| `p` | `float` | `0.0025` | structural | link probability, both initially and on rewiring; the phase parameter <br>`0` … `1` |
| `graph_updates` | `int` | `0` | population | slow-timescale steps (least-fit node replaced) applied before the network is returned; 0 returns the initial random graph <br>`0` … `20000` · *range:* the book's run finds the first autocatalytic set at update 2854 (m = 100, p = 0.0025) |
| `self_loops` | `bool` | `False` | structural | allow c_ii = 1 (direct self-replicators); the model sets c_ii = 0 |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "4 decisions"

    - The book's prose says c_ij is 'a catalytic function of species i on species j', but eq. 15.7 (x_i' = sum_j c_ij x_j ...) needs j to catalyse i. The equation is followed: c_ij = 1 becomes X_j -&gt; X_j + X_i with rate 1, under constant-total dilution.
    - The fast attractor is the Perron-Frobenius eigenvector of C, recorded as the initial state. When there is no autocatalytic set (eigenvalue 0), (C + I)^m is iterated instead, which concentrates on the ends of the longest chains. Ties for the least-populated node are broken at random.
    - After a replacement the book perturbs the remaining concentrations. That has no effect when the next attractor is computed exactly, so it is not modelled. extras.analysis records the eigenvalue and the attractor's support.
    - x0, the concentration given to a new node, only matters for numerical integration, so it is not a parameter.

## Results

### Autocatalytic sets appear inevitably and grow exponentially

Jain and Krishna (1998) ran the model with 50, 100 and 150 species and mean
degrees from 0.05 to 2.0, and tracked the number of arrows, `λ1` and the size
`s1` of the dominant ACS over the replacements. The runs they show, which they
report as typical, have three regions. First, the number of arrows hovers at the value for a random graph.
Then it rises several-fold. Then it fluctuates, in a statistical steady state,
far above its initial value. In a control run where the replaced species was
picked at random rather than as the least fit, the number of arrows never rose.

They traced the rise to one event: the chance appearance of an ACS. In their
run with 100 species and mean degree 0.25 (that is, `p = 0.0025`), `λ1` stayed
at 0 until replacement 1643, jumped to 1 when an ACS appeared, and the ACS
spanned the whole graph at replacement 2589. The Handbook chapter (Jain and
Krishna 2003), from which the book takes its figures, shows another run at
the same settings. There the first ACS is a 2-cycle between nodes 26 and 90,
formed at replacement 2854, and it spans the graph 1026 replacements later, at
3880.

They also derived the time scales. A graph without an ACS gains a 2-cycle at
the next replacement with probability about `p² s` (with `s` species), so the
first ACS arrives after about `1/(p² s)` replacements on average: 1600 at
`p = 0.0025`, `s = 100`. Since this chance is never zero, the arrival is
inevitable for any `p > 0`. After that, each new species joins the ACS with
probability about `p s1`, so `s1` grows exponentially with time constant
`τg = 1/p`, and spanning takes about `(1/p) ln(s/s1)` more replacements. The
1998 paper confirms `τg ∝ 1/m` (m being its mean degree) with a fitted slope
of −0.964 ± 0.045 on a log-log plot.

*In Chemart.* Reproduced. In the run shown under *Using it* (seed 1) the first
ACS, a 3-cycle, appears at replacement 768 and spans the graph at 2000, 1232
replacements later; the estimate `(1/p) ln(100/4)` gives about 1290. Over
seeds 1 to 8 at the same settings the first ACS appeared at 768, 1991, 592,
495, 451, 1445, 1384 and 1876 (mean about 1100, against the estimate of
1600). The test suite checks that the attractor is a fixed point of eq. 15.7
on a small hand-built graph (a 2-cycle feeding a third node, with `λ1 = 1` and
the isolated node at 0), that every reaction has the form
`X_j -> X_j + X_i`, and that a 30-species graph with `p = 0.02` has `λ1 ≥ 1`
after 1500 replacements. It does not check arrival or growth times.

### The evolved network is exponentially improbable

A graph in which every species belongs to one ACS needs at least one incoming
arrow at every node. For a random graph with the same number of arrows, Jain
and Krishna compute the probability of that as
`[1 − (1 − m*/(s − 1))^(s−1)]^s`, where `m*` is the mean degree, which falls
off exponentially with `s`. In the PNAS paper (Jain and Krishna 2001), whose
run had 117 cooperative arrows among 100 species when the ACS spanned the
graph, this probability is about 10⁻¹⁶. Yet selection builds such a graph in
about `(1/p) ln s` replacements. They suggest this may be relevant to the
origin-of-life puzzle of how highly non-random chemical organisations could
arise quickly. Chemart does not compute this measure.

### Crashes, core-shifts and recoveries

Once the ACS spans the graph, the species replaced must come from inside it.
Most replacements do little damage, but when a species that holds the
structure together goes (Jain and Krishna call it a *keystone*, borrowing the
ecological term), a large fraction of the species can die out in one step.
The system then regrows. Jain and Krishna call these three stages the random
phase, the growth phase and the organised phase; the book calls the last the
"organizing phase". The book's Figures 15.7 and 15.8 show a crash and the
resulting "boom and bust" cycles.

The Handbook chapter analyses these crashes. The core of the dominant ACS is
its irreducible part: the set of species that can each reach every other
along arrows, such as the loop in the worked example. A **core-shift** is a
single replacement after which the old and new cores share no arrow. In
1.55 million replacements at 100 species and `p = 0.0025`, there were 701
events in which more than half the species died out, and 612 of them were
core-shifts. Of the 235 events that killed more than 90%, 226 were
core-shifts. The 612 core-shifts were of three kinds: complete crashes that
left no ACS at all (136), takeovers by a new, stronger or downstream core
(241), and takeovers by a dormant loop in the periphery after the old core had
been weakened (235). Every complete crash started from a graph with
`λ1 = 1`, where the core is a single loop and every core species is a
keystone. Two conditions make a new loop take over: a larger `λ1` than the old
core, or an equal `λ1` while sitting downstream of it.

*In Chemart.* Crashes and regrowth do occur. The seed-1 run spans the graph
at replacement 2000, collapses to a 2-cycle soon after, spans again at 3948,
and suffers a complete crash (`λ1` back to 0) at 7236. Chemart does not
classify the events and was not compared with the statistics above. The first
of these collapses is also an example of a numerical problem, described below,
that makes crash timings at `λ1 = 1` unreliable.

### A classification of innovations

Jain and Krishna define an **innovation** as a new species that has non-zero
population in the next attractor, that is, one that survives until the next
replacement. The book (§15.2.3) gives a version of their classification,
noting that it differs from the authors' own:

- **Type A, short-lived.** *Blip*: a new chain in a graph without an ACS,
  which survives only by chance. *Incremental*: a parasite attached to an
  existing ACS, which draws some material but stays peripheral.
- **Type B, long-term**, which adds or changes a self-maintaining (irreducible)
  subgraph. *Independent organisation*: a new loop separate from the existing
  one, which either takes over if its `λ1` is larger (*core-shift*), creates
  the first ACS if there was none (*birth of an organisation*), or sits in the
  periphery if its `λ1` is smaller (*dormant*). *Modification of the existing
  organisation*: the new species joins the core and raises `λ1`
  (*core-enhancing*, by far the most common), or, rarely, changes nothing
  (*neutral*).

The Handbook chapter orders six types by impact: random-phase, incremental,
dormant, core-enhancing, core-shifting, and creation of the first ACS. The
book also connects the model to its own theory of chemical organisations:
autocatalytic sets are self-maintaining, and only closed ones survive in the
long run. *In Chemart:* not implemented; `extras.analysis` records `λ1` and
the attractor support, from which a user could classify events.

### What Chemart does not reproduce

- **The random phase is not random.** When the graph has no loop
  (`λ1 = 0`), Chemart approximates the attractor by applying `(C + I)` `m`
  times to equal populations. The implementation decision above says this
  concentrates on the ends of the longest chains, but after only `m` steps it
  gives every species a non-zero population, and the smallest go to species with no incoming arrow, so only
  those are ever replaced. In the model, every species not at the end of a
  longest chain has population 0 and can be replaced. As a result, arrows
  accumulate before any ACS exists: over the second half of the random phase
  Chemart's runs at 100 species and `p = 0.0025` held 44 to 69 arrows, while
  the same loop with the paper's least-fit rule held 16 to 28, close to the
  random-graph value of about 25. The arrival time of the first ACS was not
  clearly different over eight seeds. For the same reason
  `attractor_support` lists all species when `λ1 = 0`.
- **Tied eigenvalues.** When two loops with equal `λ1` sit one upstream of
  the other, the eigenvalue is repeated and the eigenvector is numerically
  ill-defined. At replacement 2001 of the seed-1 run, a 3-cycle upstream of a
  2-cycle should leave only the downstream 2-cycle populated. Chemart reports
  98 populated species, then 2 at replacement 2009, then 98 again at 2010 on
  the same pair of loops. This is the "downstream" core-shift of the Handbook
  analysis, so crash timings at `λ1 = 1` are unreliable.
- **Not modelled.** The perturbation of the surviving populations after a
  replacement (it does not change an exactly computed attractor), the small
  population `x0` given to a newcomer, and the book's figures, which are graph
  drawings from a run that cannot be regenerated.
- **The weighted model.** The PNAS paper (Jain and Krishna 2001) uses a
  different version, with link strengths drawn from [−1, 1] so that links can
  also be inhibitory, and populations clipped at zero. It reports the same
  growth, `τg = 2/p`, and limit cycles as well as fixed points. Chemart
  implements only the original model with 0/1 links, which is the one the book
  describes.

## References

Banzhaf, W. & Yamamoto, L. (2015). *Artificial Chemistries*. MIT Press. Section 15.2.2, 15.2.3; the book's bibliography entries [425], [426], [427], [428].
